subject: psych
title: Moral panic: how a society invents its folk devils
dek: Every so often a group of people, a new habit or a new medium is suddenly treated as a grave threat to a whole society. This lesson explains Stanley Cohen's idea of moral panic, follows the mods and rockers to the English seaside in 1964, and looks at later panics about mugging, comic books and satanic day-care centres.
era: Becker 1963; Clacton and Brighton 1964; Cohen 1972; Hall et al. 1978; McMartin trial 1984–1990; Goode and Ben-Yehuda 1994
honesty: This lesson is text only. The definition quoted from Cohen and the dates of the 1964 seaside clashes were checked against published summaries of Folk Devils and Moral Panics. I left out damage totals, arrest counts and newspaper headlines that I could not confirm from a reliable source, and I describe the later research in general terms.

timeline.label: The American comic-book scare
timeline.detail: The psychiatrist Fredric Wertham publishes Seduction of the Innocent, which blames crime and horror comics for juvenile delinquency. A US Senate subcommittee holds hearings the same year, and publishers create the Comics Code Authority to police themselves.

timeline.label: Howard Becker, Outsiders
timeline.detail: Becker argues that deviance is not a quality of an act but the result of other people applying a label to it, and he describes 'moral entrepreneurs' who campaign to create and enforce new rules.

timeline.label: Mods and rockers at the seaside
timeline.detail: Scuffles between groups of young people at Clacton over the Easter weekend, and at Brighton and Margate over the Whitsun weekend in May, are reported as a national crisis. Further clashes follow at Hastings over the August bank holiday.

timeline.label: Cohen, Folk Devils and Moral Panics
timeline.detail: Stanley Cohen turns his doctoral research on the reaction to the mods and rockers into the book that defines the theory of moral panic.

timeline.label: Hall and colleagues, Policing the Crisis
timeline.detail: Stuart Hall and four co-authors at the Birmingham Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies analyse the British panic about 'mugging' in 1972 and 1973 and connect it to a wider crisis of the state.

timeline.label: The McMartin preschool trial
timeline.detail: Staff at a California preschool are accused of ritual abuse of children. The case becomes one of the longest and most expensive criminal trials in US history and ends without any convictions.

timeline.label: Goode and Ben-Yehuda's criteria
timeline.detail: Erich Goode and Nachman Ben-Yehuda propose five features that mark a moral panic: concern, hostility, consensus, disproportionality and volatility.

timeline.label: McRobbie and Thornton's update
timeline.detail: Angela McRobbie and Sarah Thornton argue that the theory must change for a world of many competing media, where the accused groups can answer back and some even welcome the publicity.

blocks.text: A moral panic is a period in which a society becomes intensely and suddenly alarmed about a person, a group, a behaviour or a new invention that it sees as a threat to its values. The alarm is usually spread by the news media, taken up by politicians, police, church leaders and campaigners, and often ends in new laws or harsher punishments. When the panic passes, the threat often turns out to have been much smaller than people believed, or never to have existed in the form described.

The British sociologist Stanley Cohen gave the idea its classic definition in his 1972 book Folk Devils and Moral Panics. He wrote that societies appear to be subject, every now and then, to periods of moral panic, in which "a condition, episode, person or group of persons emerges to become defined as a threat to societal values and interests." The important word is defined. Cohen was not mainly interested in what young people at the seaside actually did. He was interested in how other people came to describe, explain and react to what they did.

Cohen called the people blamed in a panic folk devils. A folk devil is a visible, easily recognised type of person who comes to stand for everything a society fears is going wrong: the delinquent teenager, the drug user, the immigrant criminal, the corrupter of children. Once a group is cast in that role, almost anything its members do can be read as more evidence of the danger.

A moral panic does not require that the problem be invented from nothing. There were real fights at the English seaside in 1964, real street robberies in the 1970s and real cases of child abuse in the 1980s. The panic lies in the gap between the event and the reaction: the problem is exaggerated, the rare case is presented as typical, and the response grows far beyond what the evidence supports. Cohen summed this up by saying that in a moral panic the untypical is made typical.

sections.title: Labelling theory and the moral entrepreneur

blocks.text: Cohen's idea grew out of a school of thought called labelling theory, which was popular among sociologists of deviance in the 1960s. Its best-known statement is Howard Becker's 1963 book Outsiders. Becker argued that deviance is created by social groups when they make rules and apply them to particular people. A person becomes a deviant not simply by doing something but by being caught, named and treated as one.

Becker also gave Cohen a useful character: the moral entrepreneur. This is a person or organisation that campaigns to have a behaviour recognised as a serious problem and to have new rules made against it. Temperance campaigners who fought for the prohibition of alcohol were among Becker's examples. In a moral panic, moral entrepreneurs supply the speeches, the statistics and the demands for action.

Cohen worked alongside a group of young British criminologists who met in the late 1960s as the National Deviancy Conference. Among them was his friend Jock Young, who used the phrase moral panic in his own study of drug users in Notting Hill, London in the late 1960s. Labelling theory gave these scholars a key insight: the reaction to deviance can make deviance worse. If young people are treated as a dangerous gang, they may start to see themselves as one. Sociologists call this process deviancy amplification, and it is close to the self-fulfilling prophecy covered in an earlier Sunday lesson.

In early 1960s Britain, two youth styles had become easy to tell apart. Mods wore sharp Italian-style suits and long green parka coats, rode Vespa and Lambretta scooters, and listened to modern jazz, soul, Motown, ska and British rhythm and blues bands such as the Who and the Small Faces. Rockers wore black leather jackets and boots, rode heavy motorcycles, and preferred 1950s rock and roll by Eddie Cochran, Gene Vincent and British rock and roll singers such as Billy Fury. Their look owed a great deal to Marlon Brando in the 1953 film The Wild One.

Over the Easter weekend of 1964, groups of young people went to the small Essex resort of Clacton. The weather was cold and wet, there was little to do, and some teenagers scuffled, broke windows and annoyed residents and shopkeepers. Cohen, who was then a young social worker and graduate student, later concluded from police records, court reports and interviews that the trouble was real but limited, and that the division between mods and rockers was far less clear on the ground than it became in print.

The next morning's national newspapers presented the weekend as an invasion. They used words such as terror, riot and battle, described the young people as vermin and louts, and treated the two styles as rival armies. Editorials asked what was wrong with the nation's youth. Over the Whitsun bank holiday in May 1964, more clashes followed at Brighton and Margate, this time watched by reporters and photographers who had arrived expecting trouble. Further disturbances took place at Hastings over the August bank holiday. Magistrates handed out heavy fines and short prison sentences, and one described the defendants as "sawdust Caesars". Members of Parliament visited the resorts and called for tougher measures against hooliganism.

Cohen's achievement was to separate the events from what he called the inventory, the first wave of reporting that fixed the story in the public mind. He found three habits in that reporting. The first was exaggeration and distortion: numbers, violence and damage were inflated, and ordinary incidents were described in the language of war. The second was prediction: papers warned that worse was coming at the next holiday, which helped bring crowds and police to the next resort. The third was symbolisation: the scooter, the parka and the haircut became symbols that stood for delinquency, so that any young person dressed that way looked like a threat.

The reaction then fed on itself. Police forces sent extra officers to the coast and made more arrests, which produced more stories. Shops sold more parkas and scooter accessories, and some teenagers went to the seaside precisely because the newspapers said that was where the action was. In this sense the panic helped to create the very mods and rockers it described. By the late 1960s the fashion had moved on and the story faded, as Cohen predicted panics usually do.

Cohen described the life of a panic as a sequence. Something happens, or is said to have happened, and is reported. The media coverage turns it into a symbol of a broader decline. Moral entrepreneurs, such as editors, bishops, politicians and campaigners, take up the cause and offer explanations and remedies. Experts are called upon to explain why it is happening. The authorities respond, often with new policing, new laws or harsher sentences. Then the panic either fades away or leaves a lasting mark in law and in public memory.

He identified four groups that keep a panic going: the mass media, moral entrepreneurs, the control culture of police, courts and politicians, and the public. None of them needs to be lying. Journalists may simply be covering what seems like a big story, police may simply be preparing for the trouble they have been told to expect, and the public may simply believe what it reads. The panic is produced by the way their actions reinforce one another.

In 1994 the American sociologist Erich Goode and the Israeli sociologist Nachman Ben-Yehuda tried to make the idea more precise. They proposed five features that together mark a moral panic. There must be heightened concern about the behaviour of a group; hostility towards that group as an enemy of decent society; a degree of consensus that the threat is real and serious; disproportionality, meaning the reaction is far larger than the actual harm; and volatility, meaning the panic flares up quickly and dies down quickly.

items: Concern: people are worried and talk about the issue a great deal.
Hostility: a clearly identified group is treated as the enemy.
Consensus: a broad section of society agrees the threat is real.
Disproportionality: the reaction is much larger than the harm.
Volatility: the alarm erupts suddenly and fades fairly fast.

blocks.text: In Policing the Crisis (1978), Stuart Hall and his colleagues at the Birmingham Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies applied Cohen's idea to a British panic about mugging in 1972 and 1973. The word mugging had arrived from American news reports and was soon attached to young Black men in British cities. A long prison sentence passed in 1973 on a sixteen-year-old from Handsworth in Birmingham for a street robbery became a symbol of the fight against the new crime. Hall's group argued that the panic did more than reflect fear of crime. It helped a government facing economic and political trouble to build support for tougher policing, and it tied crime to race in the public imagination.

The theory also helped scholars look back at earlier episodes. In the United States in the early 1950s, the psychiatrist Fredric Wertham's Seduction of the Innocent (1954) blamed horror and crime comics for juvenile delinquency. A Senate subcommittee held hearings, and the industry responded by creating the Comics Code Authority, which for decades restricted what American comic books could show. The pattern of a new medium, an expert warning, political hearings and self-censorship would later repeat itself with rock lyrics, video games and social media.

The most damaging panic of the late twentieth century was the American and British fear of satanic ritual abuse in the 1980s and early 1990s. In the McMartin preschool case in California, members of the family that ran the school were charged with hundreds of acts of abuse, including bizarre rituals, after interviewers used leading questions with very young children. The prosecution ran from 1984 to 1990, became one of the longest and most expensive criminal trials in American history, and ended without a single conviction. Later investigations found no evidence that organised satanic abuse rings of the kind described had existed.

In 1995 Angela McRobbie and Sarah Thornton argued that the classic model needed updating. In the 1960s a few national newspapers and broadcasters could speak with one voice. By the 1990s there were many competing outlets, and the groups being accused could answer back through their own magazines, music and spokespeople. Some youth cultures and record labels even learned to court outrage, because a ban or a tabloid attack could sell records. Cohen himself accepted much of this in later editions of his book, while maintaining that the basic pattern of exaggeration and disproportionate reaction had not gone away.

sections.title: A comparison with Japan's otaku panic

blocks.text: A clear example outside the English-speaking world came in Japan in 1989, when Tsutomu Miyazaki was arrested for the murders of four young girls. Reports that his room was filled with thousands of videotapes, including horror films and anime, led much of the press to present him as a typical otaku, a word for obsessive fans of anime, manga and similar media. For several years the word carried a strong suggestion of social isolation and danger, and fans of these hobbies faced suspicion from parents, teachers and employers.

The case fits Cohen's pattern closely. A single, horrifying crime was treated as a sign of what a whole subculture was becoming, a new style of leisure became the symbol of the threat, and calls for regulation of manga and video followed. As with the mods, the label later lost much of its sting, and by the 2000s otaku culture was being promoted by the Japanese government as part of the country's international appeal.

The idea of moral panic is a powerful tool, but it can be misused. Calling a concern a moral panic suggests that it is irrational, so people sometimes use the phrase to dismiss worries that are in fact well founded. Cohen warned against this. In the introduction to the 2002 edition of his book he pointed out that some reactions that look like panics are in fact proportionate, and that the real question is always an empirical one: how large is the harm, and how large is the reaction?

For anyone running a public campaign, including a charity that wants to raise awareness of violence against women, the theory offers two lessons. First, vivid single cases move audiences, but presenting the rare case as typical can produce fear and bad policy rather than real help. Second, campaigns are most trustworthy when they give accurate numbers, name their sources and avoid turning a whole group of people into folk devils. Cohen spent his later career writing about human rights, and his 2001 book States of Denial examined the opposite problem: how societies and individuals manage not to notice suffering that is real.
Think of a recent news story that caused widespread alarm. Using Goode and Ben-Yehuda's five features, would you call it a moral panic? Which feature is hardest to judge, and why?

Cohen argued that media coverage helped create the mods and rockers it described. Can you think of a youth style, online community or fandom that seems to have been shaped by the way outsiders talked about it?
If you were writing about a real social problem for a cause you care about, how would you make people take it seriously without exaggerating it or turning a group into folk devils?

fun_fact.title: The panic became a rock opera
fun_fact.text: The seaside clashes of 1964 were turned into art less than a decade later. The Who, the band most closely associated with the mods, released the double album Quadrophenia in 1973, about a young London mod named Jimmy. In 1979 it was made into a film directed by Franc Roddam, which recreates a mod riot on the seafront at Brighton. The film gave the musician Sting one of his first acting roles, as the stylish mod leader known as Ace Face, and helped spark a mod revival among British teenagers at the end of the 1970s.
